title: Ethical and legal issues in information systems
competency: Explain the main ethical and legal issues in information systems: privacy, digital ownership, information gathering, and security and liability.

keywords.def: The discipline concerned with what is morally good and bad, right and wrong.
Keeping the personal data stored on computer systems safe from people who should not see it.
The ability to access, use and protect data, information and knowledge about ourselves or things we own.
Applications collecting users' data and credentials as part of their operations.
A person's permission before their information is collected or used.
Protecting stored and transferred information from breaches and unauthorized access.
When a third party harvests the personal details of innocent people to use them for malicious purposes.
The legal responsibility an organisation may face when information it holds is breached.

en.text: Ethics is about the principles of making right or wrong decisions; Britannica calls it the discipline concerned with what is morally good and bad, right and wrong. If ethical principles are not respected, legal consequences may follow. Many professions have ethical and legal oversight, but information systems still lack such standards because technology changes so fast.

am.text: ሥነ ምግባር ትክክልና ስሕተት ውሳኔን የሚመራ መርህ ነው። ሥነ ምግባርን መጣስ ሕጋዊ መዘዝ ሊያስከትል ይችላል።

screens.title: Right, wrong or illegal?
screens.ask: Your friend left her Telegram open on a school computer. Reading her private chats would be
opts: Wrong, and it could also become a legal issue
Fine, because the screen was open
Wrong only if she finds out
Fine if you do not share it
screens.after: Viewing someone's private information is unethical in any way. It may also end up being a legal issue.

screens.title: New technology, new questions
paras: New technologies create situations we have never dealt with before.
They can change human behaviour deeply.
They give us new capabilities that ethics has not yet addressed.
Users must know the effects of their use and access.
They must also respect the rights of creators and innovators.

screens.title: What is ethics?
paras: Ethics is about the principles of making right or wrong decisions.
Britannica: the discipline concerned with what is morally good and bad, right and wrong.
If ethical principles are not respected, legal consequences may follow.
Doctors, teachers, officials and business people have ethical and legal oversight.
Information systems still lack such standards: the technology changes too fast.
The main issues: privacy, digital ownership, information gathering, and security.

screens.title: Key word
defs: The discipline concerned with what is morally good and bad, right and wrong.

screens.text: According to the book, ethics is about
opts: the principles of making right or wrong decisions
screens.ans: the principles of making right or wrong decisions
screens.why: p.2: "Ethics is all about the principles of making right or wrong decisions."
screens.clue: Think of good and bad choices.

screens.text: Questions of ethics and legality are important in many industries, including education.
screens.why: p.2: medical and education professionals have legal and ethical oversight.

screens.text: As information technology becomes more influential, ethical and legal issues become less important.
screens.why: p.2: "The role of ethics in information systems has become more crucial as a result of technology."
screens.clue: More power brings more or less responsibility?

screens.text: Why do information systems lack standard ethical rules, according to the book?
opts: The technology changes frequently and fast
Ethics does not apply to computers
screens.ans: The technology changes frequently and fast
screens.why: p.2: information systems lack standards in "the current frequently changing and dynamic technological ecosystem".

screens.text: Which shows an ethical issue becoming a legal issue?
opts: Copying a paid app and selling it as your own
Turning off your laptop at night
screens.ans: Copying a paid app and selling it as your own
screens.why: It ignores the creator's rights (unethical) and breaks intellectual property law (legal consequences).

screens.text: A new app shows where any phone is in real time. No law covers it yet. What does the book suggest?
opts: It is a new situation; judge it ethically and keep assessing the issues over time
It is fine because no law forbids it
Only the app maker can decide
screens.ans: It is a new situation; judge it ethically and keep assessing the issues over time
screens.why: New technologies create situations not yet addressed in ethical terms (p.1); issues evolve and should be assessed over time (p.5).
screens.clue: Legal is not the same as right.

ideas.name: Privacy, digital ownership and information gathering

en.text: Privacy is about personal data stored on computer systems; viewing anyone's private information is unethical and may be illegal. Digital ownership is the ability to access, use and protect data about ourselves or things we own, so using someone's digital work needs the owner's permission. Many apps gather users' data and credentials, which raises the question of consent: always check why a service wants your data.

am.text: ግላዊነት፣ ዲጂታል ባለቤትነት እና መረጃ መሰብሰብ ዋና የሥነ ምግባርና የሕግ ጉዳዮች ናቸው። መረጃ ከመስጠትህ በፊት ለምን እንደሚጠየቅ መርምር።

screens.title: Which issue is it?
items: Someone reads your email without permission
A website posts your photo as its own work
A torch app asks for your contacts and SMS
screens.after: These are three of the four ethical and legal issues in the book. The fourth is information security and liability.

screens.title: Privacy
paras: Information privacy is about personal data stored on computer systems.
Our data is spread across many digital systems.
It should be accessed with personal passwords.
But email, social media and bank accounts can be accessed by unauthorized people.
Viewing someone's private information is unethical. It may become a legal issue.
Organisations that check employees' computer habits must not damage their privacy.

screens.title: Digital ownership
paras: Digital ownership: the ability to access, use and protect data about ourselves or things we own.
Online content is easy to copy and paste, so ownership is hard to control.
Using someone's digital work without permission is unethical.
Creators have the right to allow or deny use.
Permission promotes sharing, credits the source and protects consumers from false information.

screens.title: Information gathering
paras: Many apps collect users' data and credentials as part of their work.
This raises a debate: what may be gathered, and why?
It raises the question of consent.
Check the intention of every request for your data.
Take special care when it asks for personal details or passwords.

screens.title: Key words
defs: Keeping the personal data stored on computer systems safe from people who should not see it.
The ability to access, use and protect data, information and knowledge about ourselves or things we own.
Applications collecting users' data and credentials as part of their operations.
A person's permission before their information is collected or used.

screens.text: A flashlight app asks for your contacts, SMS and location. Which issue is this?
screens.why: The app gathers data it does not need; check its intention before giving consent.
screens.clue: What is the app trying to collect?

screens.title: Sort the scenarios
items: A colleague logs in to your bank account
A boss reads staff private messages
A blog copies your song and posts it
A student uses a cartoonist's drawing without asking
A quiz app asks for your password
A shop app records every purchase you make
screens.why: Privacy: someone sees private data. Ownership: someone uses a creator's work. Gathering: an app collects data.
screens.clue: Ask: is it seeing, using or collecting?

screens.text: Which is NOT one of the pressing ethical and legal issues in the book?
screens.why: The four issues are privacy, digital ownership, information gathering, and information security and liability.
screens.clue: Recall the four headings on p.3–4.

screens.text: Most people have their data spread through the digital world, where unintended sources can access it.
screens.why: p.3: personal accounts "can be accessed by unauthorized sources".
screens.clue: Think of how many accounts you have.

screens.text: Many people do not even realize how their personal information is being collected and used.
screens.why: p.4: many apps collect users' data as part of their operations, which raises the question of consent.
screens.clue: Do you read every app permission?

screens.text: Selam wants to use a blogger's photo in her school poster. What should she do first?
opts: Ask the owner for permission and credit the source
Use it because it is online
Change the colours and call it hers
screens.ans: Ask the owner for permission and credit the source
screens.why: Creators have the right to allow or deny use of their content (p.3).
screens.clue: Who decides how the photo is used?

screens.text: Why does asking permission before using digital content help everyone?
opts: It promotes sharing, credits the source and protects consumers from false information
It removes the need for passwords
screens.ans: It promotes sharing, credits the source and protects consumers from false information
screens.why: p.3 names three benefits of permission: sharing knowledge, crediting the source and protecting consumers from false information.
screens.clue: Think of the creator, the user and the reader.

en.text: More personal and financial data is stored and sent online, so a security breach can expose organisations to liability and lead to identity theft, when a third party harvests innocent people's details for malicious use. Accepted procedures and rules make systems more reliable. Users must report breaches promptly; in Ethiopia organisations report cyber attacks to the designated government unit, the Information Network Security Agency (INSA).

am.text: የመረጃ ደህንነት ጥሰት ድርጅቶችን ተጠያቂ ያደርጋል፤ የማንነት ስርቆትም ያስከትላል። ጥሰትን በፍጥነት ሪፖርት አድርግ፤ በኢትዮጵያ ለኢንሳ።

screens.title: Who is responsible?
screens.ask: Hackers steal a bank's customer data. Who may face legal liability?
opts: The bank that held the data
screens.after: A breach can expose the organisation that stored the data to "potential security liability".

screens.title: Security and liability
paras: Organisations store and transfer more personal and financial data online.
A breach in information security can expose them to liability.
Breaches can lead to identity theft.
Identity theft: a third party harvests innocent people's personal details for malicious use.
Blogs and instant messaging are other sources of liability.
Accepted procedures and rules make information systems more reliable.

screens.title: Report breaches promptly
paras: Users report breaches to their IT unit or expert, or the government body.
In Ethiopia, organisations report cyber attacks to a designated government unit.
That unit protects the country's information and information infrastructure.
It is the Information Network Security Agency (INSA), named on p.8.

screens.title: Reporting a security incident
steps: Notice and record what happened, when, and on which system.
Contain it. Do not delete evidence.
Report promptly to your IT unit or security expert.
The organisation reports to INSA through its official channel.
Follow the instructions and help with recovery.

screens.title: Key words
defs: Protecting stored and transferred information from breaches and unauthorized access.
When a third party harvests the personal details of innocent people to use them for malicious purposes.
The legal responsibility an organisation may face when information it holds is breached.

screens.text: When a third party harvests innocent people's personal details for malicious use, it is called
In today's digital world, locking the office door is enough to keep information secure.
screens.why: Data travels over networks, so attackers can act from far away. Procedures, rules and reporting are needed (p.4).
screens.clue: Can a hacker reach a server without entering the room?

screens.title: Order the steps for reporting a security incident
screens.why: Record, contain, report inside, report to INSA, follow up.
screens.clue: You cannot report what you have not recorded.

screens.text: Which is a common way someone gains unauthorized access to an online bank account?
opts: A phishing SMS that tricks the owner into typing the PIN
screens.ans: A phishing SMS that tricks the owner into typing the PIN
screens.why: Phishing tricks the owner into giving credentials; the others protect the account.

screens.text: Which is the most balanced view on government gathering citizens' information for national security?
opts: Allowed only by law, limited to what is needed, kept secure and overseen
screens.ans: Allowed only by law, limited to what is needed, kept secure and overseen
screens.why: Security matters, but gathering raises the question of consent and privacy (p.3–4).

screens.text: A school clerk sees a strange login to the student records system at 2 a.m. What is the best first action?
opts: Record what happened and report it promptly to the IT unit
Delete the logs to clean the system
Ignore it unless data is lost
Post about it on social media
screens.ans: Record what happened and report it promptly to the IT unit
screens.why: Users must report breaches promptly to the concerned unit or expert (p.4); deleting logs destroys evidence.
screens.clue: Who must know, and what must be kept?
